people/antony-of-egypt/summary: A Coptic Christian who, around 270, sold his inheritance on hearing Matthew 19:21 and withdrew into the desert, combating demons through prayer and fasting. Athanasius' Life of Antony made him the archetype of the desert hermit and the 'father of monks'.
people/antony-of-egypt/place/name: Monastery of St Antony, Eastern Desert
people/gregory-the-illuminator/summary: Patron saint of Armenia, said to have been imprisoned in a pit at Khor Virap for some thirteen years before healing and converting King Tiridates III. Consecrated in Caesarea of Cappadocia, he became the first Catholicos of the Armenian church, around 301 (or c. 314).
people/gregory-the-illuminator/keyIdeas/: Conversion of a nation through its king
Armenian church founded on apostolic and Cappadocian roots
people/arius/summary: An ascetic Alexandrian presbyter who taught that the Son of God, though divine and before all ages, was created by the Father: 'there was when he was not'. Condemned at Nicaea in 325 and later partly rehabilitated, he died in Constantinople before his readmission to communion.
people/arius/keyIdeas/0: The Son is the first and highest creature
people/arius/keyIdeas/1: Father alone is unbegotten true God
people/eusebius-of-caesarea/summary: Bishop of Caesarea, pupil of the Origenist Pamphilus, and 'father of church history'. His Ecclesiastical History preserves countless earlier sources; his Life of Constantine and panegyrics framed the Christian emperor as God's agent. He signed the Nicene Creed while uneasy about homoousios.
people/constantine-i/summary: Roman emperor who attributed his victory at the Milvian Bridge (312) to the Christian God, ended persecution and lavished patronage on the church. He summoned the Council of Nicaea, founded Constantinople and was baptised on his deathbed. Eastern churches venerate him as 'equal to the apostles'; others see in him the beginning of Christendom's compromise with power.
people/athanasius/summary: Bishop of Alexandria for 45 years, exiled five times, who championed the Nicene faith against Arianism. On the Incarnation argues that the Word became human so that humans might become divine; his Festal Letter of 367 is the first list of exactly the 27 New Testament books. He also wrote the Life of Antony.
people/frumentius/summary: A Syrian-Greek youth shipwrecked and taken to the court of Aksum, where he rose to high office and supported Christian merchants. Consecrated bishop by Athanasius, he returned to evangelise the kingdom; Ethiopians honour him as Abba Salama, 'Father of Peace'.
people/frumentius/keyIdeas/1: Ethiopian link to the see of Alexandria
people/ezana-of-aksum/summary: King of Aksum (reigned c. 320s–c. 360) who, tutored by Frumentius, became one of the first rulers anywhere to adopt Christianity. His inscriptions and coins move from pagan deities to 'the Lord of Heaven' and the cross.
people/ezana-of-aksum/keyIdeas/0: Royal adoption of Christianity in Africa
people/nino-of-georgia/summary: A woman from Cappadocia, remembered as a captive or pilgrim, whose healing prayers converted Queen Nana and King Mirian III of Kartli. Georgian Orthodoxy honours her as 'equal to the apostles' and enlightener of Georgia; her grapevine cross is a national symbol.
people/ephrem-the-syrian/summary: Deacon of Nisibis and later Edessa, the greatest poet-theologian of Syriac Christianity. His hundreds of madrashe (teaching hymns), sung by women's choirs, expressed doctrine through symbol and paradox rather than philosophy. He is honoured by every tradition and is a Doctor of the Catholic Church.
people/ephrem-the-syrian/keyIdeas/1: Mary and the church in typology
people/macrina-the-younger/summary: Eldest sister of Basil and Gregory of Nyssa, who turned the family estate at Annisa into an ascetic community of women and men. Gregory's Life of Macrina and On the Soul and the Resurrection portray her as the family's spiritual teacher.
people/gregory-of-nazianzus/summary: Cappadocian theologian, called 'the Theologian' in the East, whose Five Theological Orations preached in Constantinople (380) defended the deity of Son and Spirit. Briefly archbishop and president of the council of 381, he resigned and retired to write poetry.
people/gregory-of-nazianzus/keyIdeas/0: Full deity of the Holy Spirit
people/gregory-of-nazianzus/keyIdeas/1: What is not assumed is not healed
people/basil-of-caesarea/summary: Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, called 'the Great', who shaped Eastern monastic life through his Rules and founded the Basileias, a complex of hospital and poor relief. His On the Holy Spirit defended the Spirit's equal glory and helped clarify one ousia in three hypostases.
people/gregory-of-nyssa/summary: The most philosophical of the Cappadocians, brother of Basil and Macrina. He developed the doctrine of the Trinity and of divine infinity, describing the spiritual life as endless progress (epektasis) into God; some of his writings hope for universal restoration.
people/ambrose/summary: Roman governor acclaimed bishop of Milan while still unbaptised (374). He opposed Arian court influence, introduced antiphonal hymn-singing in the West, compelled Theodosius to do penance after the Thessalonica massacre and baptised Augustine in 387.
people/jerome/summary: Dalmatian-born scholar, secretary to Pope Damasus, who settled in a monastery at Bethlehem with Paula and Eustochium. His Latin Vulgate translation, largely from the Hebrew, became the Western church's Bible; he was also a fierce controversialist.
people/jerome/keyIdeas/0: Hebraica veritas (priority of the Hebrew text)
people/john-chrysostom/summary: Preacher of Antioch nicknamed 'golden-mouthed', made archbishop of Constantinople in 398. His expository homilies on Scripture and denunciations of luxury and injustice made enemies at court; he died in exile. The most-used Orthodox liturgy bears his name. His sermons against Judaizing Christians contain harsh anti-Jewish rhetoric later misused.
people/shenoute-of-atripe/summary: Abbot of the White Monastery near Sohag for some eighty years, ruling thousands of monks and nuns. He is the greatest writer of Coptic literature; his zeal against pagan temples and for the poor, and his attendance at Ephesus (431) with Cyril, made him a hero of Coptic Christianity.
people/augustine-of-hippo/summary: North African rhetor whose Confessions tell of his journey through Manichaeism and Neoplatonism to baptism by Ambrose in 387. As bishop of Hippo he wrote The City of God and On the Trinity and opposed Donatists and Pelagians. No theologian has shaped Western Christianity — Catholic and Protestant — more deeply.
people/augustine-of-hippo/keyIdeas/2: Church and sacraments valid apart from minister's holiness
people/pelagius/summary: A British ascetic teacher in Rome who urged Christians to moral perfection, insisting that God commands nothing impossible. He and his followers denied that Adam's sin is inherited and that grace is needed to will the good; Augustine's opponents condemned his views in 416–418, though scholars debate how far he held the positions attributed to him.
people/pelagius/keyIdeas/0: Human ability to obey God's commands
people/mesrop-mashtots/summary: Armenian monk and scholar who created the Armenian alphabet around 405 and, with Catholicos Sahak, led the translation of the Bible and liturgy. He is also credited with alphabets for Georgian and Caucasian Albanian.
people/cyril-of-alexandria/summary: Patriarch of Alexandria who led the opposition to Nestorius and dominated the Council of Ephesus (431). He insisted on the single subject of the incarnate Word — 'one incarnate nature of God the Word' — and on Mary as Theotokos. Chalcedonians and Miaphysites both claim him as their authority; his episcopate was also marked by violent conflicts in Alexandria.
people/cyril-of-alexandria/keyIdeas/2: One incarnate nature of the Word
people/nestorius/summary: Antiochene monk made archbishop of Constantinople in 428, who objected to calling Mary Theotokos and preferred Christotokos to protect the distinct humanity of Christ. Deposed at Ephesus (431), he died in Egyptian exile; his Book of Heraclides denies teaching 'two sons'. The Church of the East venerates him as a saint and Greek Father.
people/leo-i/summary: Bishop of Rome from 440 whose Tome to Flavian, read at Chalcedon, taught that each nature in Christ acts in communion with the other. He articulated papal primacy as Peter speaking through his successor and reportedly persuaded Attila to withdraw from Italy (452).
people/dioscorus/summary: Cyril's successor as patriarch of Alexandria, who presided over the second Council of Ephesus (449). Deposed at Chalcedon in 451 — formally for disciplinary reasons — he died in exile at Gangra. The Coptic Orthodox Church honours him as a saint and confessor of Cyril's faith.
people/dioscorus/keyIdeas/1: Opposition to the Tome of Leo
people/patrick/summary: A Romano-British deacon's son captured by Irish raiders at sixteen, who escaped and returned as a bishop to evangelise Ireland. His Confession and Letter to Coroticus reveal a humble, Bible-saturated faith and opposition to slavery. Dates are uncertain (traditionally 432–461).
people/severus-of-antioch/summary: Patriarch of Antioch (512–518) and the leading theologian of the anti-Chalcedonian (Miaphysite) churches. Deposed by Justin I, he spent his last decades in Egypt. He argued against Eutyches that Christ is consubstantial with us, and against Chalcedon that 'in two natures' divides Christ.
people/severus-of-antioch/keyIdeas/0: One composite nature of the incarnate Word
people/severus-of-antioch/keyIdeas/1: Rejection of Eutychianism and Chalcedon alike
